collection_summary: Scaled-enumeration instance built from four Wikipedia per-decade '[decade]_in_film' articles. Universe is the four decades 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, 2010s. Top-K (K=5) is applied within each decade using the 'List of worldwide highest-grossing films' table on the corresponding Wikipedia article. Result is a row-bind union of four filtered top-5 subsets — 20 rows × 5 columns. Composite PK is (Decade, Rank); 'Film' is not unique across the table because 'The Lion King' (1994) and 'The Lion King' (2019) are distinct films sharing a title.
source_coverage_notes: Single-source-family instance: four Wikipedia decade-overview articles, each contributing exactly 5 rows from its own ranked worldwide-gross table. The 1970s decade was excluded because '1970s_in_film' uses a domestic (US+Canada) gross table only, with no parallel worldwide ranking — including it would have mixed metrics in one CSV (a real curation defect). All four cited 1980s–2010s tables use the same metric, so the row set is metric-coherent. The drop of the 1970s narrows the temporal scope by one decade but yields a clean, single-metric benchmark. Wikipedia's gross figures appear to reflect lifetime worldwide gross including re-release earnings (e.g., Avatar at $2.92B includes 2022 re-release; Avengers: Endgame at $2.79B includes 2019 re-release add-ons). The top-5 ordering is stable across the 2010s and 2000s; for the 1980s and 1990s, deeper ranks (4–5) may shift with future Wikipedia edits as re-release figures accumulate, but the top-3 of each decade is robust.
decision_log: 1) Chose query_category=scaled_enumeration over top_k because the partition set itself (the four decades) must be resolved before applying top-K within each — that two-stage stress is exactly what scaled_enumeration targets. 2) Chose operation_type='union+filter' as the closest fit in the artifact-contract vocabulary; scaled_enumeration's natural primitive (partitioned top-K) does not have a dedicated operation_type value, but per-decade row-bind of top-K subsets is structurally a union over filtered sources. Documented per the artifact-contract instruction to pick the closest match and explain the choice here. 3) Excluded the 1970s decade despite the original concept covering 1970s–2010s. The '1970s_in_film' article tracks domestic-only gross (worldwide tracking was unreliable pre-1980), and no Wikipedia per-decade page provides a parallel domestic table for the 1980s onwards. Mixing metrics in one CSV would defeat the benchmark's measurement integrity, and using a Tier C source like Box Office Mojo for domestic 1980s–2010s data was rejected because Tier B Wikipedia is sufficient for a clean four-decade scope. 4) Used composite PK (Decade, Rank) rather than (Decade, Film) so that ties in rank (which would normally not occur in a top-5 by gross) are explicitly disallowed by the schema, and because rank is the load-bearing column for top-K. 5) Kept 'Year' as a separate column rather than embedding it in the film title so the year is independently evaluable as a numeric/date attribute.
normalization_decisions: Film titles follow the canonical Wikipedia article-title form for each film, including subtitles separated by ' – ' (em dash) where Wikipedia uses one (e.g., 'Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back'). Worldwide gross values are bare integers in USD with no commas, no '$' sign, and no 'million' / 'billion' suffix, per the protocol §6 numeric convention. Decade values are strings of the form '1980s' (lowercase 's', no apostrophe, no spaces). Year values are bare integers (e.g., 1982) per the protocol §6 date convention for year-only dates. Rank is integer 1–5. The two films sharing the title 'The Lion King' (1994 and 2019) are kept as separate rows; the composite PK on (Decade, Rank) ensures uniqueness without disambiguating the title.
open_questions: 1) Wikipedia's worldwide-gross figures include theatrical re-release earnings, which means the absolute values can drift over time as re-releases accumulate. The top-5 ordering is stable for the 2000s and 2010s because the gaps are large; for the 1980s (Indiana Jones #3 vs. Batman #4) and 1990s (Jurassic Park #3 vs. Independence Day #4), deeper ranks could swap if Wikipedia tables update. Periodic re-runs should diff the row set against the current source pages. 2) Wikipedia uses lifetime worldwide gross in nominal USD (not inflation-adjusted); when comparing across decades, $381M in 1985 is not directly comparable to $1.66B in 2019. The benchmark query does not require comparison across decades, but downstream evaluators should not collapse or aggregate across decades without controlling for inflation. 3) The 1980s top-5 may exclude 'Rain Man' (1988, ~$354M worldwide) and 'Who Framed Roger Rabbit' (1988, ~$329M); whether those deserve to displace 'Back to the Future' depends on which Wikipedia revision is read. The current row set reflects the 2026-04-27 snapshot. 4) 'Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace' at #2 for the 1990s reflects its lifetime worldwide gross including the 2012 3D re-release; original-release-only ranking might place it lower. 5) Future evaluation may want to exclude re-release earnings — that would be a different curation decision that should be re-staged as a sibling instance, not patched into this one.
